title: Avoidance isn't paranoia: the difference between aware and anxious
excerpt: Eleven years with the Singapore Police Force on why alert and wired aren't the same skill, the three-code framework that tells them apart, and two drills that build the sustainable one.
metaDescription: How do you stay aware without becoming paranoid? A Singapore Police veteran on the three-code system that tells alert apart from anxious.

children.text: By the time you reach your stop, your jaw has been tight for twenty minutes straight. You clocked the man who got on two stops after you, the couple arguing near the doors, the teenager who glanced at your bag twice. Nothing happened. You're just worn out, in a specific way that has nothing to do with the work day you already finished and everything to do with how hard you were watching.

I spent eleven years with the Singapore Police Force, then twenty-two more running security for MNCs across Asia-Pacific. The people I trusted most under real pressure were rarely the tense ones. They were the calm ones. Treating every stranger on a train as a live decision is a real skill, and it's also the wrong one. It spends your attention in twenty minutes flat and leaves nothing for the rest of the evening. There's a version that doesn't do that, and it's the one you can actually keep doing, for years rather than one tense commute.

Awareness and anxiety are not points on the same scale, and they don't cost the same. Awareness is a light loop you run all day, noticing what's around you and letting most of it resolve on its own. Anxiety skips that step and treats everything as a decision, which is why it runs out fast. The three-code framework below is how to tell, in your own body, which one you're actually doing.
How to be aware without being paranoid

Awareness and paranoia are not points on the same scale. Awareness is a loop: you notice what's around you, then compare it to what's normal for the place. Paranoia skips that comparison and treats every stranger as a decision that needs making immediately.

Run the loop properly and, almost every time, it resolves itself in seconds at the comparison step. Nothing was off, so nothing else happens, and you've spent almost no attention doing it. Skip the comparison and every single thing you notice becomes a live question with no answer. Awareness and paranoia notice roughly the same amount. The difference is what happens next: one lets most of it resolve immediately, the other holds onto all of it.
White, Yellow, Red: the three codes, and what each one costs

The framework I teach has three settings, and most people who call themselves safety-conscious are quietly running the wrong one. It traces back to Jeff Cooper, a US Marine lieutenant colonel and firearms instructor who set out
a four-level version of it

in his 1972 book, Principles of Personal Defense, for police officers and other armed professionals. I teach the three that do the actual work for someone without a weapon on their belt, going about an ordinary day in an ordinary city.

Code White is being unaware, absorbed in your phone or your own thoughts while the world outside your head barely registers. Code Yellow is relaxed alertness, calm but aware of roughly who and what is near you without straining to check. Code Red is action mode, focused and ready to move, built to switch off again the moment a threat clears. Most of what people call staying safe is actually an attempt to live in Code Red permanently, without ever having a specific threat to switch it off.

children.text: None of this is about which code you're capable of reaching. Anyone can reach Code Red for a few minutes, no training required, only a genuine scare. The actual skill is staying out of it until it's genuinely earned, and living in Code Yellow the rest of the time without it costing much of anything.
Why 'aware' and 'scanning for danger' aren't the same loop
Colonel John Boyd, the American fighter pilot who developed what's now called
the OODA loop

in the early 1970s, broke decision-making under pressure into four steps: observe, orient, decide, act. Fighter pilots run the loop in seconds. Someone walking through a shopping centre runs the same four steps, just slower and calmer, and they're worth knowing by name, because anxious "awareness" usually means getting stuck on the first one.

Observing is just noticing, a person crossing your path, a voice raised somewhere behind you. Orienting compares what you noticed to what's normal for the place and time. Deciding is choosing whether anything needs to change, maybe a glance, maybe nothing at all. Acting means doing it. Most of what you notice in an ordinary day resolves at orient, with the answer that this is normal here, and the loop closes before you've spent any real effort on it.

Anxious scanning skips orient. Every person becomes something to decide about, so the loop never actually closes, which is why a single evening of it can leave you as tired as an evening of real decisions would, even though almost nothing happened. The loop was never the problem. Skipping the second step is.
There's a second reason this matters beyond how your evening feels.
The signals a stranger sizing you up actually reads

have little to do with how tense you look, and much more to do with pace and attention. A person running a closed, resolved loop reads completely differently to one who's visibly locked onto every stranger in the room.
You were never built to run hot all day
This isn't a discipline problem. A 2025 paper in the journal Cognitive Science, examining decades of sustained-attention research, concludes that
perfect, unbroken vigilance isn't something any human can sustain, regardless of training or motivation

. Attention naturally cycles. Treating personal safety as a requirement to notice everything, all the time, sets a bar the researchers conclude nobody clears, not for lack of discipline, but because that isn't how attention is built.

That is, in a strange way, good news. The tight-jawed, wired-by-evening habit costs more than Code Yellow and covers no more ground, because it runs Code Red-style focus against a problem that only ever needed Code Yellow. The lighter version resolves most of what it notices in the same breath it notices it. That is the only version built to last across years of ordinary days, and ordinary days are almost all any of us get.
It's the same reasoning behind
deciding a late-night route home while you're still rested

, rather than at 1am when you're worn out. Your sharpest judgement is a limited resource, so spend it on a decision made in advance, rather than trying to force alertness later, once there's less of it left.
Two drills that build the habit, not the anxiety
Two small, unglamorous habits do more for this than any amount of trying harder to "be aware." Neither takes more than a few minutes, and neither asks you to treat anyone as a threat.

Next time you're somewhere public, spend five minutes comparing who looks alert to who doesn't, a straight back and eyes up against a slumped one buried in a phone. Notice what specifically gives each impression away. You're not judging anyone. You're training your own eye to read the same signal in yourself later.

Then, walking into anywhere new, a restaurant or a train platform, take ten seconds to silently locate the exits before you sit down or settle in. Do nothing else with the information. Most days it goes completely unused, and that's the point. It costs ten seconds, and if it's ever needed, the answer is already there.
Do both often enough and they stop being drills. They become the same kind of glance you already give a flight of stairs before taking it, old and automatic, asking nothing of you.
The three-minute habit we teach students first
packages a version of both into a single routine for the walk between two doors.
Common questions
Doesn't staying calm mean I'll notice less?

No, usually the opposite. Anxious scanning burns attention fast and taps out within an hour or two, long before most evenings are over. Calm, resolved noticing costs so little that it can run all day, which is the only way noticing more actually adds up across a whole week instead of one tense hour of it.
How do I know if I'm in Code Yellow or accidentally stuck in Code Red?

Check your body, not the room. A tight jaw and a running list of everyone nearby who might be a problem is Code Red with nothing to resolve. Loose shoulders and a general sense of who's around, without the list, is Code Yellow. The room can look identical from the outside. The difference is entirely in what your body is doing.
Is it possible to be too relaxed about this?

Yes, and that's Code White, not Code Yellow. Code White suits home, behind a locked door. It's the wrong setting for a train platform at midnight, the same way Code Red is the wrong setting for a quiet afternoon. Neither extreme is the goal. Yellow is.
Doesn't a real threat deserve more than a calm response?

It deserves Code Red, and a calm baseline is exactly what gets you there quickly, because you're not already spending your focus on a hundred non-threats when the real one shows up. Staying in Yellow most of the time is what makes shifting to Red, on the rare occasion it's genuinely needed, fast instead of exhausting.
Can I actually get good at this, or is it just personality?

It's a trained habit, not a personality trait. Every calm operator I've worked alongside learned it the same slow way, noticing an ordinary transition like a doorway or a lift and running the loop lightly there until it stopped taking effort. Nobody starts out calm at this. They arrive at it by doing it enough times that it stops being a decision.

None of this replaces training, and it was never meant to. It's the difference between reacting to every noise and running a loop that tells you which noises are worth reacting to at all, and that difference gets built the same way anything else does that has to hold up under real pressure: through repetition, with someone checking your form. That's what students build with me at
JF's programmes
